description: Эмоции, комедийная выразительность и действие. Черты героев адаптируются к эпохе, а не современный солдат в разных костюмах.
anchor:
# TubeStudio · Original expressive 2D POV history · approved visual profile v1

SCOPE: Visual design and action-driven storyboard prompts, not narration rewriting. Follow the caller's JSON schema. Never ask for CONTINUE or generate typography inside scene images.

## Drawing language (stable across episodes)
Original expressive 2D historical comedy cartoon; oversized heads, broad cheeks and softly squared short chins with individual variation; very large slightly vertical oval white eyes; simple solid dark pupils slightly larger than pinpoints; tiny curved-line noses; short thick mobile brows; simple highly expressive mouths. Bold charcoal outer contours, thinner clean interior lines, flat colors and crisp simple cel shading. No photorealism, glossy 3D, anime irises, painterly rendering, blank bean faces or tiny dot eyes. Preserve exaggerated comic acting, not realistic adult anatomy. Do not make fear or permanent eye bags compulsory.

## Era and identity (variable between characters)
A drawing grammar is NOT one recurring modern man in costumes. Adapt age, face, complexion, hair, beard, build, posture, dress, footwear, tools and accessories to region, era, season and occupation. Use warm light cream instead of gray-white for light-skinned characters, but appropriate varied skin tones for other characters. Do not impose auburn hair, modern barber cuts, shirt collars or olive uniforms on all epochs. An Upper Paleolithic Homo sapiens is an anatomically modern person, not a stooped fantasy brute; winter scenes need suitable warm clothing, not a universal sleeveless fur outfit. Avoid anachronistic materials and props. Different eras may require distinct character IDs; preserve each identity within its own sequence. Give each recurring character a fully usable description, not merely a name or asset tag.

## Composition, environment and acting
Communicate one dominant emotion and one focal story moment. Keep background cast simpler. Make faces, hands, obstacles and necessary props readable. Favor historical environments with depth but uncluttered focal action. Use muted period-appropriate bases with selective color accents; vary scene lighting and palette with place, time and mood instead of making every scene beige. Use status contrasts where relevant, not automatically. Alternate shot scales by narrative function. Thumbnail face dominance is not a rule for every video frame. Do not reproduce another creator's characters, thumbnails or distinctive compositions.

## Starting image
Write a complete standalone image prompt with rendering style, full visible character traits, era-specific dress, location, body pose, gaze, emotion, prop positions and grips, lighting, framing and free space for the planned action. Show the START before the main action, not the completed result. Include recurring asset IDs plus descriptions. No 'same as before'. Do not add modern captions or speech bubbles. Aim for concrete specificity rather than decorative adjectives. Prefer about 120–210 English words where needed, within the caller's length limit.

## Animation: action first, camera second
Design a feasible mini-event: intention → attempt → consequence → emotional reaction. For active scenes explicitly provide Start, Action, Result, Reaction, Camera and Continuity. The action must work even with a locked camera. Camera movement is optional support, not the event. Gaze, breathing, a hand twitch, dust or a slow zoom alone are not a narrative action. Use reaction pauses intentionally. One main physical action per short generated clip; do not overload with multiple fights, locations or complex hand transfers. End with a clear state that the next scene can inherit. Preserve character identity, hand assignments, number and shape of props, contact and scene geography. No disappearing objects, hand swapping or morphing. Do not add spoken dialogue/lip-sync or alter voiceover unless explicitly requested.

For genuine maps, diagrams, atmospheric inserts or deliberate reaction holds, identify the shot explicitly as Diagram, Map, Atmosphere or Reaction hold, and give it a clear explanatory purpose; do not manufacture pointless movement just to satisfy a rule. Reaction holds do not replace all action scenes. Use approximate action progression suited to the chosen model and clip duration, not guaranteed frame-exact timestamps. Prefer about 70–130 English words for detailed motion prompts, within the caller's limit.

## Production and approval
Lock a character sheet and expressions before mass generation. Test a small linked sequence with both images and motion BEFORE generating the full episode's image batch. In automated runs return the requested JSON only; the author controls batch count and approval outside the model response. A produced storyboard is a draft, not proof that character art or motion has been approved. Check the actual generated frames and clips for identity, readability, era, grips, continuity and successful action.

## Example of behavior, not mandatory story content
A soldier approaches a door with shield in left hand and sword in right. He reaches toward the handle, stops because his hand is occupied, glances at both objects and reacts with irritation. The door stays closed; items stay in their hands. This is an illustrative fictional beat, not a documented historical event. The initial still must precede the reach. Do not repeat this example in unrelated scripts.

Approved visual references are bundled under skills/2d-pov-history-style/references. They illustrate facial grammar and variation across eras, not authoritative costumes. The current storyboard text request does not automatically send these images to the language model. Apply this textual profile; do not claim to have visually inspected or attached reference files unless actually supplied.
motion: Action first: intention → physical action → visible result → emotional reaction. Begin with a drawable starting state before the attempt. Keep identities, anatomy and props consistent. One feasible action in the clip duration. Maps, diagrams and deliberate reaction pauses may stay still. Camera movement is optional and never replaces action.
